analogy.p: Imagine standing at a point on a city map, facing north (straight up the page). To give a bearing you turn clockwise, like the hand of a clock, until you face the place you want, and read the angle you turned through. Your bearing is the amount of the turn. If you then stand at the other place and turn to face back, you must turn through the same angle plus half a turn (180°), which is why the back bearing differs by 180°. It breaks down on a curved Earth over long distances, where the north lines are not parallel; GCSE assumes a flat map.

bullets: Bearings are measured **clockwise** from **north**; never anticlockwise.
Always give a bearing as a **three-figure** number: 5° is 005°, 45° is 045°, 123° is 123°.
The bearing is measured **from** a particular point: 'the bearing of B from A' means stand at A, face north, and turn clockwise until you face B.
The **north line** at a point points straight up the page (the vertical line on a map); north lines at different points are **parallel**.
A full turn is 360°, so bearings are between 000° and 360°; 360° is usually written 000°.
In diagrams the north line is marked with an N and an arrow.
The word 'from' decides which point you stand at, and the order of the letters is the single most common source of errors.
core.p: A **bearing** is a way of describing the direction from one point to another. It is the angle measured **clockwise from north**, and it is always written using **three figures**. So east is 090°, not 90°, and a bearing of 7° is written as 007°. Bearings run from 000° up to 360° (although 360° is normally written as 000°). The three-figure rule is a method-and-accuracy marker; Edexcel mark schemes often withhold the final accuracy mark if the answer is not given with three figures.

bullets: Turning clockwise: each step from one main point to the next is 90°, and each diagonal is halfway (45°).
Use these to sketch the approximate direction before measuring so that you can check that your answer is sensible.
A bearing between 000° and 090° points into the north-east quarter, between 090° and 180° south-east, between 180° and 270° south-west and between 270° and 360° north-west.
Due north is 000° (not 360° or 0°) and due east is 090°.
Diagonal directions such as NNE (022.5°) are not required, but you may be given a bearing like 022°.
core.p: The eight main compass points are spaced 45° apart, so you can write their bearings from memory. North is 000°, east is 090°, south is 180° and west is 270°. The in-between points are the diagonals: north-east is 045°, south-east is 135°, south-west is 225° and north-west is 315°. Learning these values lets you check any answer quickly: for example a point that is 'to the south-east' must have a bearing between 090° and 180°, and if you get 300° you know you have made a mistake.

bullets: **Step 1**: draw a north line (vertical) through the point you are measuring **from**, extending it well above the point.
**Step 2**: join the two points with a straight line, long enough to reach the protractor scale.
**Step 3**: place the protractor centre exactly on the 'from' point with 0° along the north line.
**Step 4**: read clockwise from north using the correct scale and write the answer with three figures.
If the bearing is greater than 180° you can measure the anticlockwise angle from north and subtract it from 360°, e.g. 115° anticlockwise gives 360° − 115° = 245°.
Check: the answer should agree with your sketch of the quarter (NE, SE, SW or NW) that B lies in.
Typical tolerance in exams is ± 2° for angles and ± 2 mm for lengths.
core.h: Measuring a bearing with a protractor
core.p: To measure the bearing of B from A you must follow a fixed procedure. Draw the north line through A, place the centre of the protractor on A with its zero line along the north line, and read the angle clockwise from north to the line AB. Because most protractors have two scales, choose the scale that starts at 0° on the north line. If the angle is more than 180° you may need to measure the other way round and subtract from 360°. Mark schemes allow a tolerance of about 2° either side, so the answer must be close but not exact.

bullets: **Step 1**: mark the starting point A and draw the north line through it.
**Step 2**: place the protractor on A with 0° on the north line and mark the required bearing (clockwise).
**Step 3**: join A to your mark with a ruler and extend the line to the right length using the scale.
**Step 4**: to add a second leg, draw a new north line at the end of the first leg and repeat.
Label points clearly (A, B, C) and write the scale on the diagram.
Convert the real distance to a drawn distance using the scale, e.g. at 1 cm to 5 km, a journey of 35 km is drawn as 7 cm.
Use the finished diagram to measure the final distance or bearing and convert the length back with the scale.
core.p: Drawing bearings accurately is a commonly examined skill. You need a sharp pencil, a ruler and a protractor. Always start by marking the starting point, then draw the north line, then measure the angle clockwise from north and mark it, and finally draw a line of the correct length. For scale drawings convert the real distance to a length on paper first. Do not rub out construction lines: they show your method.

bullets: 'Bearing of B **from** A' : north line at **A**, angle clockwise to AB.
'Bearing of A **from** B' : north line at **B**, angle clockwise to BA.
'Sails **on a bearing of** 070° **from** the harbour' : the north line is at the harbour.
'Walks from P **to** Q' : the bearing is of Q from P.
'Returns to the start' means the journey back uses the back bearing.
In a question with three points, work out which point each bearing is measured from before drawing anything.
Sketch first, then add north lines at every point mentioned.
core.h: Reading the wording: 'the bearing of B from A'
core.p: The wording is critical. 'The bearing of **B from A**' means the direction you would face to go from A to B, measured at A. 'The bearing of **A from B**' is the direction from B to A, measured at B, and it will be a different number. A common error is to draw the north line at the wrong point. A reliable habit is to underline the word after 'from' in the question, because that is where the north line is drawn and where the angle starts.

bullets: If the bearing is **less than 180°**, back bearing = bearing + 180°. Example: 065° gives 245°.
If the bearing is **greater than 180°**, back bearing = bearing − 180°. Example: 250° gives 070°.
Reason: **parallel north lines**, so alternate (or co-interior) angles give the 180° difference.
Check: a bearing and its back bearing always differ by exactly 180°.
Another check: if you went north-east (045°), coming back must be south-west (225°).
In an exam write the working, e.g. '065° + 180° = 245°', for the method mark.
You may also be asked for the back bearing as part of a longer journey (e.g. a ship returning to port).
core.p: The **back bearing** is the bearing of the starting point as seen from the finishing point, i.e. the direction for the return journey. If the bearing of B from A is known, the bearing of A from B is found by **adding 180°** if the first bearing is less than 180°, or **subtracting 180°** if it is greater than 180°. The reason is that the north lines at A and B are parallel, so the angle between the line and the south direction at B equals the original angle (alternate angles), and the bearing is 180° plus that angle. In short, the back bearing points the exact opposite way.

bullets: Parallel north lines: **co-interior angles add up to 180°**, so the angle between a north line and a path plus the angle on the other north line equals 180°.
Alternate angles: the angle between a path and the south direction at one point equals the angle between the path and north at the other end.
The interior angle at a turning point is often 360° − (bearing in) − (180° − bearing out) or can be found by sketching.
Angles around a point: the bearing, the angle inside the triangle and the remaining angle add up to 360°.
Isosceles triangles (equal distances) give equal base angles, which can lead to a bearing.
Always show the reason: 'co-interior angles', 'alternate angles', 'angles in a triangle sum to 180°'.
Add the angle to or subtract it from the bearing you know to get the new bearing, then check by sketching.
core.p: Many bearing questions need angle facts rather than a protractor. The north lines at the different points are all parallel, so you can use **alternate**, **corresponding** and **co-interior** angles. You also use **angles on a straight line (180°)**, **angles around a point (360°)** and **angles in a triangle (180°)**. Where two legs of equal length appear the triangle is isosceles, so its base angles are equal. The key is to mark every north line, mark all the angles you know, and then find the angles inside the triangle.

bullets: Scale 1 cm to 5 km: a drawn length of 6.4 cm represents 6.4 × 5 = 32 km.
Ratio scale 1 : 50 000: 4.6 cm on the map is 4.6 × 50 000 = 230 000 cm = 2300 m = 2.3 km.
Always state units and convert between cm, m and km carefully (100 000 cm = 1 km).
To draw a journey, choose a convenient scale, draw each leg with a north line, then measure the final distance and bearing.
Accuracy: use a sharp pencil, measure to the nearest millimetre and the nearest degree.
If the question gives a scale drawing already, check the scale given before measuring.
Answer in context, e.g. 'the ship is 32 km from the port'.
core.p: Bearings often appear with maps and scale drawings. A **scale** such as 1 cm : 5 km, or a ratio such as 1 : 50 000, links the distance on paper to the real distance. To find a real distance multiply the measured length by the scale factor and convert units. Convert units carefully: 1 km = 1000 m = 100 000 cm. You will usually be asked to measure the distance or bearing from your own accurate drawing, and your answer is accepted within a stated tolerance.

bullets: Distance by Pythagoras: c² = a² + b², where a and b are the north-south and east-west legs.
Angle from north: tan θ = east-west distance ÷ north-south distance (opposite ÷ adjacent, with north as the reference line).
8 km east and 6 km north: distance = √(8² + 6²) = 10 km and θ = tan⁻¹(8 ÷ 6) = 53.1°, so the bearing is 053°.
For a point to the south-east, the bearing is 180° − θ if θ is measured from south, or 090° + θ if measured from east.
For a point to the south-west, bearing = 180° + θ (θ from south); for the north-west, bearing = 360° − θ (θ from north).
Always draw a sketch with the north line first, to see which angle you are finding.
Round the final bearing sensibly (nearest degree unless told otherwise) and give three figures.
core.h: Calculating distances and bearings: Pythagoras and trigonometry
core.p: When the journey is made of legs along north-south and east-west lines, you can calculate rather than draw. The legs form a right-angled triangle, so use **Pythagoras' theorem** for the straight-line distance and **tan** (or sin or cos) for the angle. Remember the final step: the angle from trigonometry is usually measured from the north line or the east line, and you may need to add or subtract to turn it into a three-figure bearing measured clockwise from north.

bullets: **Cosine rule** for a side: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A (use when you know two sides and the included angle).
**Cosine rule** for an angle: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc (use when you know all three sides).
**Sine rule**: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B (use when you know a side and its opposite angle plus one more angle or side).
Ships leaving P at 040° for 12 km and at 120° for 9 km have an angle of 120° − 040° = 80° between their paths, giving AB² = 12² + 9² − 2 × 12 × 9 × cos 80° = 187.49, so AB ≈ 13.7 km.
To find the bearing of B from A: sin A ÷ 9 = sin 80° ÷ 13.69 gives angle A ≈ 40.3°; then the bearing of B from A is 220° − 40.3° ≈ 180° (using the back bearing 040° + 180° = 220° of P from A).
Remember: the angle between two bearings from the same point is their difference (or 360° minus the difference if it is more than 180°).
Area of a triangle: ½ ab sin C is sometimes needed in area-of-land problems.
Keep full calculator values until the final answer to avoid rounding errors.
core.h: Higher tier: sine and cosine rule with bearings
core.p: At Higher tier, bearings are combined with the **cosine rule** and **sine rule** for triangles that are not right-angled. The bearings give you an angle between two legs (the **included angle**), and you may also know two distances. First draw a clear sketch with north lines, then use the difference of the two bearings (or angle facts) to find the angle in the triangle, then apply the correct rule. To find a bearing from a calculated triangle angle, you add or subtract it from a known bearing, and you often need the back bearing in between.

bullets: A journey with legs 060° then 150° makes a 90° turn: the second bearing minus the first is 90°, so the legs are perpendicular and Pythagoras applies.
The turn at a corner is the difference between the outgoing bearing and the back bearing of the incoming leg.
To find the total displacement, break each leg into north and east components using sin and cos if needed: east = d sin(bearing), north = d cos(bearing).
**Loci**: a point equidistant from two places lies on the perpendicular bisector; bearings help to draw this accurately.
**Vectors**: a bearing and distance describe a vector; adding journeys is adding vectors.
**Ratio and scale**: converting map distances uses the same ideas as enlargement.
**Trigonometry**: SOH CAH TOA applies once you identify the right-angled triangle.
Check final answers for sense: a plane flying NE cannot end up south of its start.
core.h: Typical contexts, multi-leg journeys and links
core.p: Bearing questions are wrapped in contexts such as ships and aircraft, hikers and orienteering, search-and-rescue and surveying. A multi-leg journey (for example, 'A to B on a bearing of 060° then B to C on a bearing of 150°') needs a diagram with a north line at each turning point and the angles at each point worked out one by one. Questions often ask for the distance and bearing of the end point from the start, which needs Pythagoras or the cosine rule. Bearings also link to loci (equidistant from two points), vectors (direction), ratio (scale), and similar triangles.

exam: **Three-figure bearings** are needed in the final answer; the accuracy mark is often lost for writing 45° instead of 045°.
**Measure/draw questions** (2 to 4 marks): bearing within 2°, lengths within 2 mm. Show the north line and construction lines.
**'Work out the bearing of A from B'** (usually 2 marks): quote the back bearing rule and show 'bearing ± 180°' working.
**With reasons** (3 to 4 marks): state alternate or co-interior angles because north lines are parallel, and give the angle facts in words.
**Scale questions**: show the conversion line, e.g. 6.4 × 5 = 32 km, and give units.
**Pythagoras and trig** (3 to 5 marks): draw a right-angled triangle first. M1 for the correct formula, M1 for substitution, A1 for the value.

**Cosine and sine rule** (Higher, 4 to 6 marks): label the triangle, state the rule used, substitute, and keep full calculator accuracy; give the answer to 3 significant figures unless told otherwise.
**Multi-step bearing questions (6 marks)**: sketch with north lines at every point, find the triangle angles with reasons, then use trigonometry; show each step clearly.
Check that your bearing agrees with the compass direction (e.g. south-east means between 090° and 180°).
If a diagram is given, add the north lines and mark every angle you find on it.
Calculator in degree mode; check this before using trig functions.

mistakes.r: Bearings are always measured clockwise from north.
For 'the bearing of B from A' the north line and angle are at A, the point after 'from'.
mistakes.w: Drawing the north line at the wrong point

mistakes.r: Back bearing = bearing ± 180°: add 180° if less than 180°, subtract if more.
mistakes.w: Giving the back bearing as the same angle or as 90° different

mistakes.r: Subtract 180° instead. A bearing never exceeds 360°.
mistakes.w: Adding 180° to a bearing that is already above 180° to get a number over 360°

mistakes.r: Sketch the north line and add or subtract the triangle angle to get the clockwise angle from north.
mistakes.w: Using the angle from the triangle as the bearing without checking the direction

mistakes.r: Convert carefully: 1 km = 100 000 cm. Answers need the right units.
mistakes.w: Not converting units from the scale (cm to km)

mistakes.r: Use the cosine rule (Higher) unless there is a 90° angle.
mistakes.w: Using Pythagoras on a triangle without a right angle

mistakes.r: The angle must be the included angle between the two known sides.
mistakes.w: Using the cosine rule with the wrong angle

summary: A bearing is a direction given as an angle measured clockwise from north, always written with three figures (e.g. 045° or 270°). You must measure and draw bearings accurately, work out back bearings, use angle facts about parallel north lines, and combine bearings with scale drawing, Pythagoras, trigonometry and (Higher) the sine and cosine rules to find distances and directions. It is a favourite multi-step topic that rewards careful diagrams.

terms.d: The direction of one point from another, measured as an angle clockwise from north and written with three figures.
A line pointing straight to north at a point; north lines at different points are parallel.
A bearing written using three digits, adding zeros at the front if needed, e.g. 045° or 007°.
The direction of turning in which the hands of a clock move.
The bearing of the starting point from the finishing point, found by adding or subtracting 180°.
One of the standard directions N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.
The ratio of a length on a drawing or map to the real length it represents.
An accurate drawing in which every length is in the same ratio to the real lengths.
An instrument used to measure and draw angles in degrees.
Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet; north lines are parallel.
Equal angles in a Z-shape between parallel lines.
Angles between parallel lines on the same side of a transversal; they add up to 180°.
The angle between two known sides of a triangle.
a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, used to find a side from two sides and the included angle, or an angle from three sides.
a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C, used when a side and its opposite angle are known.
The straight-line distance and direction from the start point to the end point of a journey.

worked.q: (a) The bearing of B from A is 072°. Work out the bearing of A from B. (b) The bearing of P from Q is 305°. Work out the bearing of Q from P. (3 marks)
steps: Check (b): 125° and 305° differ by 180° ✓, and 125° is south-east, opposite to north-west 305° ✓. [A1]

worked.q: A hiker walks 8 km due east from P to Q, then 6 km due north to R. (a) Work out the distance PR. (b) Work out the bearing of R from P. Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures where appropriate. (5 marks)
steps: Angle at Q is 90° (east meets north), so use Pythagoras: PR² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100. [M1]
Angle between the north line at P and PR: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 8 ÷ 6 (east distance over north distance). [M1]
R is north-east of P, so the bearing is 053°. [A1]

worked.ans: (a) 13.7 km  (b) 180° (more precisely 179.7°, so B is almost due south of A)
worked.q: Two ships leave a port P at the same time. Ship A sails 12 km on a bearing of 040°. Ship B sails 9 km on a bearing of 120°. (a) Work out the distance AB. (b) Work out the bearing of B from A. Give your answers to 3 significant figures. (6 marks)
steps: Sine rule for angle PAB: sin A ÷ 9 = sin 80° ÷ 13.69, so sin A = 0.6473 and A = 40.3°. [M1]
Bearing of P from A (back bearing) = 040° + 180° = 220°. Bearing of B from A = 220° − 40.3° = 179.7°, i.e. 180° to the nearest degree. [A1]
